claims.text: Phase-selective recrystallization annealing can simultaneously increase strength and ductility in eutectic high-entropy alloys.
The intervention selectively recrystallizes the soft phase while preserving a skeletal hard-phase network.
The relevant initial alloy has a duplex microstructure containing distinct soft, ductile and hard, strength-providing phases.
The relevant initial state may be as-cast or conventionally processed.
A thermal annealing protocol can be designed to recrystallize the soft phase without altering the hard-phase network.
There is an approximate reported annealing-temperature range in which only the soft phase recrystallizes.
The expected improvement should hold under quasi-static room-temperature mechanical testing.
The treatment produces a fully recrystallized soft phase embedded within a hard-phase skeleton.
The hard-phase skeleton remains unaltered during the treatment.
Selective recrystallization enhances strain hardening through the soft, deformable phase.
The preserved hard-phase skeleton retains alloy strength.
The phase-selective microstructure changes strain partitioning between the two phases.
Changed strain partitioning can overcome the conventional strength-ductility trade-off.
Relative to an untreated or conventionally annealed eutectic HEA, the treated alloy will have higher yield strength.
Relative to an untreated or conventionally annealed eutectic HEA, the treated alloy will have higher ultimate tensile strength.
Relative to an untreated or conventionally annealed eutectic HEA, the treated alloy will have greater uniform elongation.
The proposed benefit is limited to alloys possessing clearly distinct soft and hard phases.
Overly aggressive annealing may cause complete recrystallization or coarsening and negate the intended benefits.
Optimal annealing temperature and duration and the magnitude of improvement vary with alloy composition and processing history.

Failure to obtain statistically significant improvements in both strength and ductility, or failure to verify selective recrystallization with an intact hard-phase network, would falsify the hypothesis.
